settings.title: Every workflow declares a mode
settings.body: AUDIT analyses and changes nothing. PLAN sequences findings. IMPLEMENT makes one named change. VALIDATE confirms it worked. Never letting one session both find and fix is the single convention that makes the rest of the toolkit work.
settings.code:
> **Mode: AUDIT** — this workflow changes nothing.
>            It produces findings.

settings.title: Discovery runs first, then stops
settings.body: The master audit reports the site's structure, the conversion architecture and what it cannot determine without data you have not given it. Then it waits. You read it before anything else happens.
settings.code: ### Phase 1 — Discovery. Change nothing, then stop.

settings.title: Findings carry evidence and an honesty label
settings.body: Thirteen fields, including the one that matters most: is this a proven problem, a strong heuristic, an experiment opportunity, or insufficient data? A heuristic never becomes proof because it was written confidently.
settings.code:
Evidence: iPhone 13, Safari 17, 390x844. Focusing
#card-number raises the keyboard; submit sits at
y=812, under it. Reproduced 3/3.
Type: proven problem

settings.title: Priorities are scored, and some things are marked do-not-do
settings.body: Impact × Confidence ÷ Effort, each 1–5, banded into this week, this month, next quarter, and do not do. Two rules override the score: critical severity jumps the queue, and measurement comes first.
settings.code:
| Purchase event never fires | 5 | 5 | 1 | 25 | This week |
| Hero headline is vague     | 3 | 2 | 1 |  6 | Experiment |
| Button colour inconsistent | 1 | 2 | 1 |  2 | Do not do |

settings.title: Tracking is verified in both directions
settings.body: An event that fires on the real action is half the check. The other half is proving it does not fire on page load, on a refresh of the confirmation page, on back-navigation, or on a client-side route change. Duplicate purchase events make every downstream number wrong in the same direction.
settings.code:
Positive: complete an order -> exactly 1
Negative: refresh confirmation -> 0
          back-navigation      -> 0
          SPA route change     -> 0

settings.title: The experiment workflow that tells you not to
settings.body: Before designing a test, a gate: is it broken, is it a requirement, would you ship it regardless, and do you have the traffic? For most sites the answer is that testing is impractical — and saying so beats three weeks producing a number nobody should act on.
settings.code:
Under 100 weekly conversions — no useful A/B testing
100–500  — very large effects only, rarely
Above 500 — a programme becomes possible

settings.title: It refuses the tactics you did not ask for
settings.body: Fake countdowns, untracked stock warnings, invented customer numbers, hidden fees, pre-selected add-ons, confirmshaming, obstructive cancellation. The prohibition is repeated in every workflow, because a rule stated once at the start of a long session does not survive to the end of it.
settings.code:
Would this still work if the visitor understood
exactly what was happening?

settings.question: Will this increase my conversion rate?
settings.answer: Nobody can promise that and this does not. What it does is find the places a site loses people, rank them by evidence rather than by opinion, and give you a way to tell whether each fix worked. Where the honest conclusion is that a site does not have enough traffic to know, the workflows are written to say so — which is more useful than a number produced to satisfy the question.

settings.question: How is this different from the SEO toolkit?
settings.answer: The SEO toolkit gets people to arrive. This one works out what happens to them once they do. They share no material: the SEO toolkit has no conversion coverage at all, and this one defers search-performance analysis to it rather than duplicating it.

settings.question: How is this different from the Launch System?
settings.answer: The Launch System builds and launches a site, and contains one landing-page CRO workflow among its 100 prompts. This is 70 workflows on conversion alone, plus funnels, analytics, experimentation and user research, none of which the Launch System covers. If you are building a site, start there. If you have one that under-converts, start here.

settings.question: Do I need an analytics platform for this to be useful?
settings.answer: It is considerably more useful with one, and the toolkit is explicit about that. Where you have no measurement, the workflows mark the affected findings insufficient data rather than guessing, and the first recommendation becomes instrumentation. That is the correct order, and there is a full module on setting it up.

settings.question: Does it work if my site does not have much traffic?
settings.answer: Yes, and it is written for that case. Most sites cannot run a useful A/B test, so the toolkit's route is defect-fixing, qualitative research and judgement — with an explicit workflow whose job is to tell you when testing is not viable and what to do instead.

settings.question: Which platforms does it cover?
settings.answer: Shopify has a module that reads the theme source rather than only the rendered page. WooCommerce, Webflow and Squarespace, and JavaScript frameworks each have their own file. Everything else applies anywhere. Every platform file states what is fixable in the theme, in an app, in settings, or not at all.

settings.heading: Conversion is the third of four problems
settings.intro: This toolkit assumes the site exists and people arrive. Building it, getting it found, and keeping it running are the other three jobs — or take the first three together.
settings.note: Each solves a different stage. The whole lifecycle is explained here if you are not sure which you are in.
